title: Our duty to praise
hookLine: once a High Holy Day prayer, now said at the end of every service

cards: Morning, afternoon or evening, the last few minutes of a synagogue service tend to sound alike. People stand. The tune picks up.
And at one line, the room bends its knees and bows, together. It sounds like an ending that was always there. Historians say otherwise.

For a long stretch, this prayer belonged to Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, in the solemn season of the High Holy Days. Then, sometime in the Middle Ages, it moved out of the High Holy Days and into every single day.

teach.b: Its first word is aleinu: it is upon us, it is our duty. The opening says, roughly, it is our duty to praise the Master of all, to give greatness to the one who formed the world.

teach.h: WE BEND THE KNEE AND BOW.
teach.b: Then the bowing line: and we bend the knee and bow and give thanks before the King of kings. That's when people bow. Where did it come from?

teach.h: FROM ROSH HASHANAH TO EVERY DAY.
teach.b: Some scholars connect it with the sage Rav in Babylonia, who is said to have arranged the Rosh Hashanah prayers about God's kingship; Aleinu opens that section.

On the High Holy Days it keeps its old drama: in many synagogues the cantor, and sometimes everyone, kneels and lowers all the way to the floor, a posture the rest of the year's prayers don't ask for.
The second paragraph turns outward, toward a hope: a day when the world will be repaired under the kingship of God.
The Hebrew phrase there, l'taken olam, to repair the world, is one of the roots of the modern words tikkun olam.
It ends with a verse from Zechariah, in the old Jewish translation: "And the LORD shall be King over all the earth; in that day shall the LORD be One, and His name one."
So the prayer moves in two steps: our duty to praise, right now, on our knees, and the hope that one day the whole world will join in. The service ends holding both.

how: Aleinu is said standing at the end of the morning, afternoon and evening services, and many people bend the knees and bow at the line about bending the knee; on the High Holy Days many congregations kneel and prostrate fully during it.

games.q: you're standing at the end of the service, saying Aleinu. you reach the words we bend the knee and bow. what does the room do?
games.why: people bend their knees and bow at those very words; on the High Holy Days some go all the way to the floor.

practice: Stand, if you can, and if you pray, say the opening in your own language: it is our duty to praise.
At we bend the knee and bow, do just that, knees soft, a bow from the waist, then come back up slowly and stand a moment, letting your body remember what it just said.

wordCard.voice: Aleinu. It is upon us. The prayer of duty and hope that closes the service, with a bow in the middle.

orig.note: Hebrew: it is upon us, our duty. the first word of the closing prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: bow now, and hope later. A week of Tachanun, the ark opening, the yad, lifting the scroll, the haftarah, Mi Sheberach and Aleinu. That's day six hundred two.
